# Complex Projective Plane and Cross Ratio

## Projective Plane
::: {#def}
Given sets $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{L}$, we call the elements in $\mathbb{P}$ points, and the elements in $\mathbb{L}$ lines. Given a subset $\mathcal{I}$ of $\mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{L}$, then for a point $P$, define $\mathbb{L}_P=\{\ell\in \mathbb{L}\mid (P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}\}$; for a line $\ell$, define $\mathbb{P}_{\ell}=\{P\in \mathbb{P}\mid (P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}\}$. If $\mathcal{P}=(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{L},\mathcal{I})$ satisfies

(1) For all points $P$, $|\mathbb{L}_P|>1$; for all lines $\ell$, $|\mathbb{P}_\ell|>1$.

(2) For any two distinct lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$, there exists a unique point $P$\in\mathbb{P}_{\ell_1}\cap \mathbb{P}_{\ell_2}$, we write $P=\ell_1\cap \ell_2$.

(3) For any two distinct points $P_1,P_2$, there exists a unique line $\ell\in \mathbb{L}_{P_1}\cap \mathbb{L}_{P_2}$, we write $\ell=P_1P_2$.

then $\mathcal{P}$ is a projective plane.
:::

::: {#lem-bezout}
## Bézout's Theorem
Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ be two projective plane curves in $\mathbb{CP}^2$ of degrees $d_1$ and $d_2$ with no common components. Then
$$
\sum_{P \in C_1 \cap C_2} I_P(C_1, C_2) = d_1 d_2.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the resultant of the defining homogeneous polynomials $F$ and $G$:
$$
\operatorname{Res}(F, G) = 0
$$
Thus the intersection is non-empty. $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {#rem-coord}
## Homogeneous Coordinates
Note that $(X:Y:Z)$ are defined up to a non-zero scalar multiple.
:::

As shown in @lem-bezout and @rem-coord, intersection multiplicities are well-defined.
